growth_story.headline: Nepal's income per person grew 3.1 percent a year over 1990–2025 through conflict, an earthquake and unrest, carried by remittances more than jobs at home.
growth_story.arc: The data show one long era: since 1990, income per person in Nepal has grown 3.1 percent a year with no lasting shift up or down. The World Bank splits these years into a Maoist conflict from 1996 to 2006 that disrupted the economy and sent workers abroad, a post-war stretch of unstable governments to 2014 that brought no growth surge, and a run of shocks from 2015. Income per person grew 3.8 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 3.5 percent over 2016–2025, but the later decade swung hard: flat in 2016 after the earthquake and India's blockade, 8.8 percent in 2017 and 7.4 percent in 2018 as rebuilding lifted investment from 27.6 percent of GDP in 2015 to 33.8 percent in 2019, then a 4.2 percent fall in 2020 with COVID-19. Across these years, money sent home by Nepalis working abroad kept household spending up and poverty falling, even as exports and industry stalled. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, the same year youth-led protests forced the prime minister to resign.

threads.title: Conflict, then no peace dividend
threads.text: A Maoist insurgency from 1996 to 2006 disrupted the economy and pushed workers abroad. Peace in 2006 did not bring a growth surge: frequent changes of government and a long wait for a new constitution held back the economy.

threads.title: Earthquake, blockade and rebuilding
threads.text: Income per person was flat in 2016, after the 2015 earthquake and India's border blockade. Rebuilding then lifted investment from 27.6 percent of GDP in 2015 to 33.8 percent in 2019, and income per person grew 8.8 percent in 2017, before COVID-19 brought a 4.2 percent fall in 2020. The World Bank notes that the investment went mostly to reconstruction rather than new industries.

threads.title: Remittances carry spending, not exports
threads.text: Money sent home by Nepalis working abroad has cut poverty and supported millions of households. The World Bank finds it has also pushed up local prices and the real exchange rate, wearing down the price edge of exports, while industry has stalled and jobs at home have been slow to come.

threads.title: Unrest and a new government
threads.text: Youth-led protests against corruption in September 2025 turned into wide unrest and led the prime minister to resign. In the uncertainty that followed, services growth barely picked up and new investment was held back. A snap election in March 2026 gave one party a majority.

since_last_year.text: Youth-led protests in September 2025 led the prime minister to resign, and a snap election in March 2026 gave a single party a majority. Conflict in the Middle East, where most Nepali migrant workers are based, weighed on the outlook in early 2026. In August 2026 a flood in Rasuwa damaged hydropower, power lines and transport, and the World Bank now expects growth to slow in FY27.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes 2015–2023 as years of repeated shocks. Yet in the data, income per person grew 3.5 percent a year over 2016–2025, close to the 3.8 of the decade before, and 2017 and 2018 were the two fastest years in a series that starts in 1960. The same report ties much of the rise in investment after 2015 to rebuilding after the earthquake rather than to new industries, and investment has since fallen back to 23.6 percent of GDP in 2025.
